*Guideline 5.1.1*

_The primary function of a Bolt app is to connect passengers with drivers in a safe and reliable manner. Ride-hailing services inherently depend on user identity verification for safety, accountability, and payment processing. This is necessary for:_

* _ensuring the safety of both riders and drivers;_
* _preventing fraudulent transactions;_ 
* _ensuring compliance with transportation and public safety regulations;_
* _allowing drivers to identify riders upon pickup._

_The Bolt app is also used for the provision of car-sharing and micromobility services. Many jurisdictions have legal requirements for operating shared vehicles, such as:_

* _age restrictions;_
* _driver’s license verification; and_
* _insurance compliance, which often requires identifiable user data._

_The guideline states that apps may require personal information if it is "directly relevant to the core functionality of the app". In the Bolt app, requiring a name, phone number, and payment details is not an arbitrary request but an essential operational requirement. Requiring user registration is directly relevant to the core functionality of the app._

*Guideline 2.1* 

*What face data does the app collect?*

_The app collects plain images of users' faces (selfies) and does not process or store biometric data. Instead, we share user selfies with our trusted verification provider to verify the authenticity of submitted images, which includes subsequent processing of facial measurements._

*Provide a complete and clear explanation of all planned uses of the collected face data.*

_To verify the identity of our users, namely to ensure that the user's selfie shows a clear face and matches the face on their identity document. Face images are being used to:_ 

* _detect the presence of the face on the image;_ 
* _detect the liveness of the image (the fact that image is not a picture of the picture, or picture of the device screen etc.); and_ 
* _compare with the face on an image of the users’ document (like ID card or passport)._

*Will the face data be shared with any third parties? Where will this information be stored?*

_The captured images of the face are being passed to Amazon AWS Rekognition service via API to perform checks mentioned in the answer to the previous question. Images are being stored securely in Amazon S3 bucket in the Central Europe zone (Frankfurt)._

*How long will face data be retained?*

_We store users' selfies for as long as they have an active account or have requested their personal data to be deleted in accordance with the GDPR._ 

*Where in the privacy policy is the app’s collection, use, disclosure, sharing, and retention of face data explained? Identify the specific sections in the privacy policy where this information is located.*

_Global Privacy Notice for Passengers:_ [https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/privacy-for-riders/|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/privacy-for-riders/|smart-link] 
_Section “4. What purposes do we use your personal data for and what is our legal basis for processing?”, specifically under the “To authenticate your account and verify your identity” point_

*Quote the specific text from the privacy policy concerning face data.*

_"We collect information to verify who you say you are and in certain circumstances to verify your age and eligibility for a Bolt account, when required by local law. If we ask you to verify your identity (either upon registration or as a result of unusual activity being detected on your Bolt account) and you are not able to verify, the Bolt services will be suspended to prevent fraud until the verification process is completed. As part of the verification process, you may be asked to submit a selfie and/or ID document to prove your identity._

_To verify your identity quickly and securely, we use facial recognition technology to confirm that your selfie shows a clear face and matches the face on your identity document. This involves processing your facial measurements._

_Your biometric data may be shared with trusted verification providers to confirm your identity. If you prefer not to use facial recognition technology, you can opt for your identity to be manually verified by a member of our team, though this may take longer. You can withdraw consent at any time by contacting our Customer Support._

_We retain your selfie and identity document as long as you have an active user account."_

_and_

_"Consent - Your opt-in consent will be required in order for us to proceed with biometric verification checks."_

{quote}In Linux, page faults occur when a program tries to access a page of memory that is not currently in physical RAM. There are two types of page faults: *minor page faults* and *major page faults*. Here’s the difference between the two:

*Minor Page Fault*

* *Definition*: A minor page fault occurs when the page is not in memory, but the page is still available in the system's swap space or resides in a file (like a memory-mapped file).
* *Handling*: The operating system can quickly retrieve the page from the disk without needing to perform any I/O operations that involve swapping. This typically involves updating the page table and possibly moving the page from disk cache to RAM.
* *Performance Impact*: Minor page faults are relatively fast to handle since they do not involve the overhead of swapping data between memory and disk.{quote}

Thank you [~accountid:63da287e790148a18093a774] !  The food cost document generated from Bolt system is not an official invoice/receipt.  [~accountid:712020:0d141639-a418-4182-bf79-da810d7a35a7], is food summary document not sending to eaters, under both B2C and B4B Food?  

# Invoice to whom?
The document mentioned, it is concerning the individual eaters as they need an official invoice to get reimbursements from their employers (companies).  

* To be clear, in this case, individual eaters are the customers to the providers, i.e. contracts of selling food is concluded between the eaters (not the companies) and the providers.  Hence, providers are invoicing the individual eaters, not the company.   Even if the eaters later ask for a reimbursement (not subject to VAT) from the company, the company incurs an expenses that’s not subject to VAT and no need to report in their VAT returns.
* Also, for sales within Latvia that do not exceed a tax value of 150 euros, the Latvian VAT Law allows for the issuance of a simplified invoice (only required supplier name, VAT number, sale amount, VAT amount, etc.). Similarly, if the tax value is equal to or less than 30 euros, a cashier’s receipt may be provided instead (no buyer name).  Therefore, in practice, customers receive an invoice/receipt with transaction details and supplier details, not themselves own information.  

# Discount?

* If the discounts funded by Bolt, then they are not presented in providers' invoices.  
* But providers received the same amount as per the invoices (as Bolt will compensate them with the discounts funded by Bolt to eaters) and report the same for VAT reporting purpose.  
* The details of discounts are shown on the Bolt Food App order page.  So I assume, the individual eaters will get reimbursement on how much they actually paid.

h1. Issue Analysis

HTTP/2 protocol error occurred when the content-length header was set to a non-zero value, but the {{DATA}} frame was empty (length: 0) with {{End Stream}} flag set. This triggered Envoy to respond with {{RST_STREAM}} and {{PROTOCOL_ERROR}}.

h1. Root Cause

The issue was identified in the NJSC framework's stream handling mechanism:

# Request payload: We were piping the stream from {{.parsePostData}} into {{ClientHttp2Stream}}
# On {{NGHTTP2_REFUSED_STREAM}} error, we’re attempting to retry the request with a new ClientHttp2Stream
# However, the original stream was already consumed during the first attempt, resulting in an empty payload during retry

h1. Solution Implemented

# Primary Change: Switched to buffer-based payloads for most requests to ensure reliable retry capability
# File Upload Exception:

* Maintained stream-based approach for file uploads.
* Added {{Expect: 100-continue}} header.
* Implemented payload streaming only after receiving {{Continue}} response.

Regarding 1.7.1. - I’m sorry, I don’t speak French, so I have to ask - is it worded as Bolt will forward drivers' personal details to Axa. That would be the preferred option in my view. I can check with LOPS what is the current setup. 



Regarding 1.14. - Is this clause in general compliant with the principles of French Civil Law (i.e. do you see similar contract clauses often, or is this rather extraordinary)? Based on the limited context, it is hard for me to tell, whether it is an issue for us or not. As long as it is not non-compliant, I think it is fine? 



Regarding 3.3. - So this is a more a complicated matter. I have provided some details in the Google Doc that I linked above as well. However, in short, according to El Khomri, platforms have to provide certain social securities for self-employed drivers. The drivers on our platform are categorised in two groups: 1) individual drivers and 2) fleet drivers. However, fleet drivers can be materially differentiated further - a) self-employed fleet drivers and b) fleet-employed fleet drivers. So according to El Khomri Bolt is obligated to provide coverage for 1) individual drivers and 2a) self-employed fleet drivers. However, as it stands today, Bolt does not have the mechanism to differentiate fleet drivers. So what we agreed with Axa in principle is, that Bolt will report the km’s for individual drivers and fleet drivers (without the differentiation). However, the drivers who are eligible for compensation are only individual drivers and self-employed fleet drivers (the drivers will be asked a proof of employment status during claim process). Fleet-employed fleet drivers shall not be covered by this policy, as they should claim from the policy that is provided to them by their employer. This will help us to keep the claims costs lower (and therefore negotiate a better price during next renewal), but also, if we ever achieve a differentiation mechanism, and it is able to provide retrospective overview, then we can receive rebate from Axa. The key issue is, how to make sure that the contract reflects what has been agreed. 



If some of these topics require a further discussion, I propose having a quick call 🙂 



Best 

Karmel

h2. [*Bundled consent approach*|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FGU2c5i84Gbd5vu5G0MZeKekaHW1g7NFJ6NMcx9GYps/edit?gid=1299470294#gid=1299470294]

Users will be asked to consent to a broad, bundled consent screen covering both *selfie-check verification* and *duplicate/fraudulent account detection* purposes. This approach aims to reduce potential user hesitation while still obtaining the necessary consent for biometric verification.Key Considerations

* *Risk & Compliance Concerns*:
** This method poses risks as it *does not ensure clear and informed consent*, which may not align with regulatory best practices.
** The broad wording might be challenged for *lack of transparency*, as users may not fully understand what they are agreeing to.
** Data Protection Authorities (DPA) could *question the validity* of the consent process.
* *User Handling Based on Consent Choice*:
** *Users Who Consent*: Their biometric data will be used for both *selfie-check verification* and *duplicate/fraudulent account detection*.
** *Users Who Decline*: They will undergo *manual verification* for selfie-checks, and no biometric data will be stored or checked against a database.

While this alternative approach offers a way to proceed with the project, it carries legal and reputational risks due to concerns over transparency and validity of consent. If challenged, Bolt may need to revise the consent process to meet regulatory expectations. That's why we need *formal approval from management* to launch the project.

h2. *Testing*

This approach involves conducting biometric verification tests without obtaining user consent, particularly in less-regulated markets and high-risk, non-EU countries. The goal is to test the system in a way that remains invisible to users while ensuring seamless onboarding without disruptions.Key Considerations:

* The tests will be conducted in *specific countries*, prioritising those with *less stringent data protection laws*.
* *Users will not be notified* about the testing process, and their onboarding experience will remain unchanged.
* No users will be *blocked or affected operationally* as a result of the test.
* *Deletion* of all data after testing
* Duration: 4-8 weeks

h1. Root Cause Analysis

* The alert for out-of-order metrics was triggered during Envoy Pod rolling restarts.
* The issue stemmed from using Pod names as identifiers instead of Pod IPs in metrics.
* During rolling restarts, two Pods temporarily exist with the same name:

# The terminated Pod (in "Terminating" state)
# The newly created Pod (in "Starting" state)

* This caused metric confusion as both Pods were reporting under the same identifier.

h1. Solution Implemented

* Added {{kubernetes_pod_ready}} label to Envoy metrics.
* This new label helps distinguish between:
** Ready Pods ({{kubernetes_pod_ready="true"}})
** Terminating/Starting Pods ({{kubernetes_pod_ready="false"}})

h1. Verification

* Tested during subsequent Pod rolling restarts.
* Confirmed metrics are now properly ordered.
* No false alerts are triggered during Pod replacements.

*Summary on AKI 2032:*

Bolt received a termination notice from AKI on 18th of February.

In the termination notice, Bolt received a reprimand from AKI for violation of Article 7(3) of the GDPR on the basis of Article 58(2)(b) of the GDPR. Supervisory procedure was closed by AKI. AKI notes the following:


# Where an opt-out link is used to refuse an offer in a free and easy way, it must be ensured that the opt-out link works.
# If the customer himself approaches the controller for assistance to opt-out of direct marketing because the opt-out link does not work or the opt-out link is missing, the controller must, if he so requests, manually opt-out of direct marketing himself and not direct the customer to further use other electronic interfaces (e.g. an app) if the customer does not so request.

As a result of AKI's reprimand, Bolt will implement changes to its CS process to readily unsubscribe data subjects from marketing when complaints relating to unsubscribe from marketing are received. Currently, as a first step, Bolt's CS directs users to Communication preferences in the application, so they can unsubscribe themselves. If the user is unsuccessful, only then manual unsubscribe is done.

[~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d]  - I've issued a request to the CS content team (CCM-20091) to update our guidelines in accordance with AKI's request - you were added to the ticket. Let's coordinate in Slack if you have any questions re/ this.

*Internal notes on the impact of the case:*

# AKI's confirmation of Bolt's violation of Article 7(3) - withdrawal of consent - is important for us as it confirms again that AKI sees "soft opt-in" as based on "consent" lawful basis, and not "legitimate interest" lawful basis.
# This understanding of AKI was first established in the light of AKI 1798 inquiry which was closed in July 2024. This interpretation means that unsubscribes from direct marketing must be treated as "withdrawal of consent" under Article 7(3), and not as "objection requests". This, in turn, necessitates more stringent standards for unsubscribe requests, i.e. Bolt must always provide a simple and effective option to unsubscribe from all direct marketing.
# The change in the unsubscribe logic is already being discussed with the Bolt's marketing team in #lcm_privacy_risk_mapping - audit trail in this ticket. More updates on this will follow in March.
# *Audit trail note:*
## Cognito tracker updated.
## Jira ticket updated.
## Slack updated.
## Drive updated.

As a next step, while not explicitly requested by AKI, I intend to follow up with AKI and send a short confirmation that our CS procedures were updated per their recommendation once implemented.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h2. 🇵🇹 🚗 RFI Form 23 Requests

*Use the issue:* Fleet Owner > I want to request a document

h3. About the RFI form

Fleet owners typically request the "Certificado de Residência Fiscal" or RFI Model 21 at the beginning or end of the year. This annual request is crucial as it certifies our fiscal residence outside Portugal, ensuring that VAT (IVA) is not applicable for transactions between EU-based companies.

By obtaining the Modelo RFI 21 and a certificate of Bolt’s address, fleet owners can provide necessary proof to the tax office that no VAT was charged on their transactions. This documentation is vital for complying with EU tax regulations and helps fleet owners avoid double taxation and unnecessary VAT charges on their earnings.

In case you receive a ticket regarding the RFI Form, follow the steps below: 

h3. Fleet Owner requests an RFI form

* Open an empty document of the _Modelo RFI_ to your computer
** If you do not have an empty _Modelo RFI_ document, reach out to your TL
* Fill in box VI on the RFI with the name and NIF (VAT) number of the Fleet, and save the document
** You can find this information in Admin Panel in Rides > Fleets > Companies
** If you cannot find the fleet with the FO’s e-mail, look for past fleet tickets or ask the FO directly
* Send the RFI to the Fleet Owner
** Delete the filled-in document from your computer
** Mark the ticket as _Solved._

----

Things to note about this form and the process:

* Bolt charges commission on each ride and sends an invoice to drivers/fleet owners regarding this commission.
* Before 1st December 2018, the invoice was issued from Taxify BV (located in Holland). After 1st of December, it is issued by Billify OÜ (Estonia) and after 7th of May 2019, it is issued by Bolt Operations OÜ.

Hey Steve,

Following our call :

# *FRA Annual Leave* should be distinguished in 2 types of leave :

* *CP N* : which is a balance that accrue 25/12 =2,0833 each month, starting January and total to 25 in December of the same year (if employee worked a full year). They don’t “expire” end of December of same year, they are just transferred to CP N-1 balance.
* *CP N-1* : which is a balance that is garnished each January, based on the total of CP N accrued over previous year. They expire as of end December of same year.

# For *starters/leavers*, please apply the below :

_a._ *_RTT_* _&_ *_CP N_* _pro-rata for_ *_starters/leavers,_* _both_ *_daily_* _and_ *_hourly based_*_:_
_Monthly acquisition /30 * number of calendar days of employment in the month, then rounded up to 2 decimals._

b. So for each day of below listed leaves, it impacts the monthly accruing of monthly RTT as below :

*Impacting rule:*
_RTT normally acquired in the month / number of working days in the month * number of working days actually worked, rounded up to 2 decimals._

*List of leaves concerned :*

* Unpaid Leave
* GBL sick leave
* GBL Occupational Injury Sick Leave
* ESP BEL FRA ITA POR Paternity leave
* GBL Maternity Leave
* GBL Parental Leave

About tax evasion - we already report courier earnings to tax authorities. In cases when courier does not have individual activity certificate, Tax authorities simply charge courier with higher income rates.

- For Individual activity couriers the rate is 5-15% (depending on annual earnings amount)

- For people, who were identified not having an individual activity certificate during the quarter when earnings were received: income tax rate is 20% (and treated as “other, irregular income”)

So all of them eventually have to pay taxes, it’s just courier responsibility to issue that Individual Activity Certificate to pay lower taxes.

This is the way I see it (and what I’ve seen in tickets from couriers after Y2023 declaration). I could also sync with VMI once again to make sure that is exactly what happens. Hi, Evelina,

 

Before answering your question, once again I have to remind that I‘m not a legal expert, therefore my comment cannot be perceived as legal advice.

 

In general, that could be an option, because you, as a service provider (intermediary) can claim, that in contactless delivery courier is not serving the client. On the other hand, if courier cannot find doors/entrance/place and she/he cannot contact (call) the client – what should he/she do? There might be technical solutions to translate messages or smthg, but again it is up to the client if he/she is accepting it.

 

Once again, this law sets requirements for couriers as individually working persons, not for the platforms, therefore legally there are no obligations for Bolt. On the other hand, we do understand that this is public pressure for Bolt to ensure services in Lithuanian, and if this “requirement” is not fulfilled another draft law could be made in a near future.

 

Probably, there might be an option to have for example three options:

* Delivery service in Lithuanian;
* Delivery services in English (for foreigners who lives in LT);
* Contactless delivery (for those who does not care);

 

In this case, you will create a possibility for a client to chose and therefore lower the public pressure.

 

Hope this does help.

** (1) Download the driver’s data via the data export tool, which should show what data we still have about them. Do not provide this to the driver - this is just a reference point.

** (3) Based on the categories of data you have found, check their purposes of processing in Section 4. Then, check if any of these purposes would still apply after account deletion (see Section 8) - these are the purposes we are interested in.
** (4) In the response, list the categories of data and the purposes of processing after account deletion, per the following examples. Ensure the language is closely aligned with the drafting in the updated privacy notice. As an FYI, detecting fraud and responding to legal claims are likely to apply to every category of data that you identify

Hello [~accountid:61cc1c959ee70a00680edd89] [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] [~accountid:712020:7bba2b49-0587-4c16-9423-0d1c64c4b359] 

The right or possibility to collect the unpaid amount from another payment method used by the same customer for other Bolt services (Bolt Food and Ride-Hailing) depends primarily on the terms and conditions agreed upon by the customer. If Bolt Drive T&Cs explicitly allow Bolt to recover unpaid amounts from any payment method linked to the customer’s account, we are legally entitled to proceed with charging the other payment method. 

Moreover, we also have to consider local regulations (such as the EU’s Payment Services Directive 2) may impose restrictions on charging a different payment method without additional authorization. However I wont think of this as the main risk. 

I’ll say the highest risk is related to chargeback & dispute risks. If the customer files a chargeback/disputes the transaction with their bank or card issuer. Having our contractual rights and transaction history properly documented are our way of defending against such chargebacks claims.

# Reviewing product overview document
# Reviewing previous experiments

So to conclude based on my observations:

* *There is not much sense in us handling driver blocks* - why? - 
** because we will not really gain from penalizing the drivers
*** What would be the purpose of the block? - to stop top accounts sending out inappropriate (scammy/phishing/negotiation) messages
*** What would the purpose of fraud control? - that we can block faster and have option to say stop this guy? - We are not really time sensitive in this scenario as we don't really ‘stop’ financial fraud here. For sure, we can’t start with action on the first indication of someone else’s model feedback so everything is delayed anyways hence there is no rush that only we can ‘solve’. 
*** We would classify ourselves as very fancy middleman - fraud will not have the last or primary gain here - it would be marketplace quality who would like their supply to be clean, professional and present a good image toward other customer groups. 
** because it will require operational management that our team can’t effectively offer
*** Important to also look forward - what happens when there is a block applied? - someone will need to follow up on it either to regain control of a potentially stolen account (as where the schemes of scam are most prevalent, it is more friction to create driver accounts than to take them over) or to review the block upon a complaint. 
**** In these scenarios - the fraud team will not have any insight other than ‘yes these chat flags’ triggered. We don't have access nor expertise to review if the driver account has been recovered. We also don't have an operation resource/process to review legitimacy of suspensions as it would require for us to know chat specifics which in any scenario does not make sense to duplicate into
*** What happens when the blocking machine gets introduced - these blocks would be under fraud name and cost but we are not in a role here to gain from the suspensions. It would require us to manage (training, info, data collection) these cases under blocking engine. 

*So in my conclusion, driver suspensions should not be managed by Fraud as they solve a behavioral problem of driver's account user attempting(!) [chat trigger <> success] to personally gain.*  These cases rather fit under the decisions happening under quality team. 

* We already have a system in place that communicates with the quality team - we *could* define flags for them to read similarly like with other matters
** Should we? If the chat and quality could communicate directly then would prefer them to make their decisions together



*Fraud’s gain for drivers from the project:*

* We could gain additional understanding regarding order behaviour - why for example there would be issues with pricing, and or flow of things
* We could gain additional signals to decide if the driver payout should go out automatically



*Impact:* 

* I expect these cases to be low impact in grand scheme - few major scenarios relating to some drivers

The possibility of charging other payment methods is not 100% expressly stated in the [Bolt Drive Platform T&Cs for PT|https://bolt.eu/en-pt/legal/tnc-bolt-drive/?category=boltDrive], but it gives us some room as explained below.

* Users must register a payment method for in-App payments (clause 5.3) - referred to as Selected Payment Method. This in theory should encompass the case of users who registered multiple payment methods.
* Users authorise Bolt to debit this Selected Payment Method and must ensure there are sufficient funds available (clause 5.4).
* Bolt can implement other collection procedures and the costs are transferable to the user (clause 5.7). I’d say that charging another payment method is less onerous for the user than going to court or using a debt collector, for example, which comes with extra costs.
* *Users agree to add new Selected Payment Method if Bolt’s ability to collect sums is jeopardise (clause 5.8). This is our strongest argument T&Cs wise in my opinion.*

*Finally, another very strong argument is that, based on the information in this ticket, the user is clearly at fault because they stole the car and this has been reported to the police. So it’s not the typical case of a dispute where it’s tricky to establish or prove the user’s responsibility.*

Hello [~accountid:6052892160d39e006f72f166], thank you for providing additional context to this request. I will formulate my feedback here below in French to facilitate the use of french terms.

----

En respectant la législation française, une personne détenant un titre de séjour “salarié” ne peut pas ouvrir une micro-entreprise ou devenir auto-entrepreneur. Ce titre de séjour est accordé uniquement pour une activité salariée et ne permet pas d’exercer une activité indépendante ([https://www.welcometofrance.com/fiche/cst-travailleur-temporaire-et-salarie|https://www.welcometofrance.com/fiche/cst-travailleur-temporaire-et-salarie|smart-link]).

Les modalités de la création d’une micro-entreprise ou d’un statut auto-entrepreneur sont régis par le Code de commerce. Lors de la demande d'immatriculation sur le guichet des formalités des entreprises, il faut indiquer un certain nombre d'informations et joindre des documents justifiant de la situation de la personne.  

{quote}_Nul ne peut être immatriculé au registre s'il ne remplit les conditions nécessaires à l'exercice de son activité. Les personnes morales doivent, en outre, avoir accompli les formalités prescrites par la législation et la réglementation en vigueur les concernant._ ([Article L123-2 du Code de Commerce|https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000006219284]){quote}

Cette obligation doit être respectée, sous peine de sanctions.

{quote}_Le fait de donner, de mauvaise foi, des indications inexactes ou incomplètes en vue d'une immatriculation, d'une radiation ou d'une mention complémentaire ou rectificative au registre du commerce et des sociétés est puni d'une amende de 4500 euros et d'un emprisonnement de six mois._

_Le tribunal compétent peut, en outre, priver l'intéressé, pendant un temps qui n'excède pas cinq ans, du droit de vote et d'éligibilité aux élections des tribunaux de commerce, chambres de commerce et d'industrie et conseils de prud'hommes._ ([Article L123-5 du Code de commerce|https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000025559438]){quote}



*Pratique de Bolt:*

* Dans le cas où, une personne veut s’inscrire en tant que chauffeur indépendant et se présente avec un kbis de sa micro-entreprise et un titre de séjour “salarié”, sa situation n’est pas conforme à la législation française et nous ne devrions pas accepter son inscription sur la base que sa situation est irrégulière et non-conforme à la legislation française.
* Pour minimiser nos risques, il faudrait que les agents soit instruits à cette notion et leur demander d'être attentifs à l’occupation sur le titre de séjour des individus qui souhaitent s’inscrire en tant que chauffeur indépendant pour s’assurer qu’ils ne détiennent pas un titre de séjour salarié. 
* À noter, que Bolt n’est pas à l’origine de l’irrégularité et n’est pas en faute lorsqu’une personne fait une demande d’inscription avec un kbis valide pour justifier de son statut. Cependant, d’un point de vue compliance, il ne faudrait avoir que des chauffeurs indépendants qui sont en conformité avec les exigences règlementaires. 

Pourrais tu inclure cette mention dans la page que vous avez sur confluence: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/FROPS/pages/4233724797/Que+faut-il+renseigner+v+rifier+sur+les+profils+chauffeurs|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/FROPS/pages/4233724797/Que+faut-il+renseigner+v+rifier+sur+les+profils+chauffeurs|smart-link] ? Je peux relire le texte avant publication si besoin. 

----

Happy to discuss this further if you have more questions. 

Thank you !

Thanks all - I appreciate the conflict between transparency and our legal position on this. As such, given that this kind of activity is limited to airports only (which lowers the privacy risk profile), we can lean in favour of the Legal considerations over the Privacy ones. I have tweaked the Privacy position below on this basis.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Conclusion:*

In light of competing legal issues, and given that the risk profile of the feature is low - If it will not be feasible to proceed with the feature with the UI integration, we can *green-light* the feature without it from a Privacy POV.
{panel}

*NOTES*

* FIFO queues are generally not as high risk for us, as they are limited in geographic scope (i.e., airports). However, as we are all aware, we are getting some heat in the UK about how it is not always fully clear to drivers how work is being allocated to them, and so any new features that we roll out in this context (particularly where the processes are fully automated, as they naturally are here) have a heightened risk profile. Overall, I would say that this feature is {color:#ff991f}*moderate risk*{color}.
* The main concern with this feature from a Privacy POV is with *transparency*. In light of the heat we are currently getting in the UK, we would ideally de-risk this feature by ensuring we are being transparent *_enough_* about how this work re work allocation without revealing confidential information about our algorithms. Proceeding without this creates transparency risk.
* However, we appreciate the Legal issues re penalising drivers. As such, if it will not be feasible to proceed with the feature with the UI integration, we can take a risk-based approach and go ahead without it. We can also consider updates the Privacy Notice from our side.
* However, I am also keen to hear the answer to Alex’s point regarding whether any UI language is possible, as this would of course be preferable from a Privacy POV.

*_As a general rule, the DPA and Regulations require reporting_* {color:#bf2600}*_only where_*{color} *_the risk has been categorized as_* {color:#bf2600}*_“high”_*{color} *_after your internal assessment._* {color:#006644}*_Once you have put in place mitigation measures such that the residual risk is no longer high, then you can proceed with the processing activity._*{color} *_In the event the assessment results in a high risk, you are required to submit the DPIA first and then request for consultation or guidance as you submit. The Regulator would only be able to offer guidance once the final report is presented for its scrutiny._* 

*_If the risk is_* {color:#006644}*_categorized lower_*{color}*_, there is_* {color:#006644}*_no need for consultation_*{color} *_under the DPA. It is very clear that only high-risk categorized assessments should be submitted._* 

However, they advise implementing additional mitigation measures to reduce the risk, including:

* *Record driver's concerns:* Seek and document privacy concerns from a selection of drivers, and if this is not appropriate to document the reasons in the DPIA.
* *Inform drivers:* Inform drivers in the privacy notice that they may be recorded, and enforce this in their terms and conditions.
* *Control over data:* Provide individuals with control over their data, such as through consent → I think this may not be applicable in our case, where we rely on legitimate interest for both riders and drivers, but please let me know what you think.
* *Control over data:* Ensure both drivers and riders can raise DSRs.
* *Children's data:* Address considerations for processing children's data captured in recordings.
* *Issues of public concern:* Investigate any potential public concern issues related to this processing.
* *Access period vs. Bolt Retention period:* Specify the retention period for recordings on Bolt’s side. 
* *Training of relevant Bolt staff:* Conduct training for relevant staff on handling the recording data.
* *Inform users about the training:* Include information about this training in the privacy notice for riders and drivers.
* *Opt-out option:* Consider an opt-out option for drivers, if appropriate, and document the reasoning if not implemented.
* *DSR:* Include this processing in the DSR procedure in case users request recordings (both drivers and riders).
* *Sharing with third parties:* Add the risk of sharing recordings with third parties (e.g., law enforcement) to the DPIA.

So far, what we had pelias-pip-active deployments have:

# Init container → Upload ~8Gb from jfrog and unpack it, took ~9 minute.
# Main container → On startup service processing files which was upload from init container, took ~12 minutes to startup. 
# Container also failed due to probes failing, had not enough time to startup. 

After tests, kudos [~accountid:610279937ab143006ecfb2ee] for hints, was made following actions: 

* Switched underlying EC2 disks to faster one (ebs->nvme), also deprecated pelias ec2nodeclass with tunned EBS.
* Bump CPU limits (not significant changes in costs, due to enough free CPU on nodes, pod have big RAM requests anyway creates a big nodes). 
* Replace wget with curl + pipe forwarding to zstd 
* Adjusted probes to not fail container early then loaded features

So as a result: 

# Init container → Decreased 9 to 3 minutes. 
# Main container → Startup decreased from 12 to 8-5 minutes (same as local env)
# Fixed probes → Containers not killing early, but startup fast enough to not be blocked by probes

# What is in place at Bolt Business to ensure privacy compliance
# What Must be in place at Bolt to ensure privacy compliance

h1. *Summary:*

----

h3. *1. Existing Bolt Business Customers*

* All data-sharing activities, including those related to Bolt Lux, are covered under Clause 4 of the standard[ Bolt Business T&Cs|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/legal/?category=boltBusiness].
* This clause broadly outlines the separate responsibilities and controller status of the customer and Bolt regarding personal data processing.
* It includes basic collaboration clauses on data breach notifications and data subject rights requests under privacy laws.

Compliance status - :green-check: 

----

h3. *2. Existing Riders*

* All data processing activities are covered under the existing Passenger Privacy Notice, which:
** Explains how Bolt processes data when a ride is taken.
** Details how data is processed when a ride is ordered by a business customer.
* The notice does not differentiate between different ride categories (including Bolt Lux or premium categories), as there is currently no distinction in data processing activities.

*Compliance status* - :green-check:  as long as no additional data processing activities for passengers are conducted. Will have to be revised to accommodate future plans of Bolt Lux service development, i.e. a separate application for Bolt Lux.

----

h3. *3. Fleets*

* A general privacy compliance gap exists, as the current T&Cs do not include relevant clauses on data sharing with fleets.
* The Privacy team is working on adding these clauses to the standard fleet T&Cs in Q1-Q2 2025 - its an ongoing clauses.
* These clauses will also be incorporated into agreements with Bolt Lux fleets, with minor adjustments for the Bolt Lux context.

*Compliance status* - not fully ensured at the moment - in progress :arrow_right_orange: 

----

h3. *4. Drivers*

* Bolt regulates the processing of driver personal data through its privacy notices, including tracking practices.
* This includes drivers that operate independently as well as with fleets.
* No changes are required unless Bolt introduces additional monitoring or data collection from drivers.

*Compliance status* - :green-check: as long as no additional data processing activities for passengers are conducted. Mayl have to be revised in the future to accommodate future plans of Bolt Lux service development.

If Bolt starts collecting sensitive personal data (e.g., vaccination, criminal record), consent may be required. Bolt still will be responsible under the data protection law - however, it can push its responsibility to fleets in some cases.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h4. *Future Compliance Considerations*

*Additional reviews will be necessary for any new activities in Bolt Lux involving personal data processing. For example, this may include:*

* Conducting assessments to confirm and document Bolt’s right to process personal data (lawful basis).
* Documenting new processing (i.e. purposes, retention, other details) in our records.
* Ensuring data subject rights under privacy laws can be satisfied where required (e.g., right to deletion if requested).
* Ensuring that data sharing with third parties (in addition to fleets) is properly protected in the contract. Any third parties specific to Bolt Lux that will process personal data must be flagged and recorded.
* Calculating and documenting risks to data subjects when legally required - e.g., additional monitoring of drivers that may be perceived as intrusive.
* Security of personal data – for a new product features or vendors, an Infosec review must be requested - [https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/17|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/17|smart-link] .
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
h4. *Bolt’s Data Security & Handling Procedures*

*Standard data security and processing of personal data are outlined in:*

* [Security Notice|https://bolt.eu/en/security/]
* [Privacy Notice|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/] - portal.

Internal documentation can also be found in Confluence / Drive.
{panel}

Ran a super generic pattern based on the status behaves vs distances driver in comparison to the ‘total’ journey. 

* compare distances between client location and driver arrival → misuse of “waiting for client” distance that accumulates paid wait 
* compare distances between client location and trip start → should be already “driving with client” instead. 

If we see that driver has arrived a significant distance away and then started the trip quite a distance away then then we can make a safe assumption that extra charges were accumulated due to early and late behaviour and the paid wait applied would be an overcharge due to the fault of the driver. 

Let’s check all cases where there was paid wait applied to the order.

*Arrivals - meters between driver ‘arrived’ and rider location:*
We can see that the higher higher we go with the distances, the more weight paid wait has on the changes. Interestingly, the price increases correlate pretty stably to the paid wait as well as the extra distance from arrival.  

!Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 21.47.36.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 21.47.36.png"!

*only showing first 2km but the distances go as far as 194km.


*Departures - meters between driver ‘driving with client’ and rider location:*
As can be seen, the higher we go with distances, the more rare cases get as well as the more stable are the numbers. This means that from a higher distance between the parties, the lower the chance of hurting the driver earnings with our decisions. 

!Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 21.44.12.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 21.44.12.png"!

*only showing first 2km but the distances go as far as 194km.
Now we’d need to separate the cases that do not make sense to charge vs those that are just driver clicking through statuses → RDNH cases where removal of paid wait is redundant really or cases where it is just super small. 

Both cases show quite the decrease within the first hundredths - which is very logical - not always the pickup happens EXACTLY at the location nor the location may be accessible and rider may move from the time of ordering. Hence the couple of hundred meters definitely do not tell us much.  

Hence, let’s focus on cases that have more than 400meters. 

!Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 22.29.52.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-24 at 22.29.52.png"!

So it is visible that the first groups of paid wait charges affect a lot of orders but gain very little if deciding to remove these fees. High friction, low gain. It normalizes around the 30 thb range where we really start seeing the distinct scenarios.

On any implications for the case, Wiersholm has also added: 

We believe it might be advantageous for Bolt that the Norwegian Taxi Association ("NT"), which is supposed to be an available association for all license holders, to take a side in this matter. The fact that NT wishes to represent the state in the case and claims that both the obligation to affiliate with a taxi centre and the taximeter requirement are important for its members, might indicate that our assumptions about this being a political game, where the established taxi centers control the market, are correct. In this context, it is also interesting that one of the main goals of NT is to "Work for equal competitive conditions" while simultaneously choosing to assist the state, which has just enacted competition-restricting legislation. In our view this involvement could potentially undermine the state's credibility when it claims that the new laws are based on purely objective considerations and is not a political battle.

The possible disadvantage of involvement, however, is that NT has been involved in the taxi market since 1919, and in this way, enjoys a certain credibility due to its knowledge of the market's challenges and development. The association can also assist the state with a lot of facts and statistics.

Overall we believe that this situation appears somewhat strange for the state and clearly signals that the legislative changes are, in fact, a political battle aimed at protecting large, established taxi centers in the market.

We are not so sure that the lawyers of the Government is pleased by the fact that the Taxi Association is a so called Amicus Curia in this case. They have probably not been asked. We know from other cases that they prefer not to have such politically motivated helpers

NT's financial crisis could certainly also motivate the association to support the case in a manner that is most economically beneficial for them. It is reasonable to assume that most of the association's members are license holders from established taxi companies who still favor the requirements for taximeters and central affiliation. This also suggests that it is economically advantageous for the association to support the new legislative proposals. However, we have not yet found data to confirm this. Consequently, it is currently challenging to assess whether this information is strategically useful, but it may become relevant as the case progresses.

** *acceptance_rate and driver_score* – minimum values of Acceptance rate and Driver Score
** *ppr* – point per ride
** *ppr_peak_hours* – points per ride in peak hours
** *loyalty_targets* – minimum points driver has to get for the tier
** *peak_hours* – peak hours by weekday in UTC timezone

*I have a question about Bolt Rewards*

The Bolt rewards program offers discounts and rewards for drivers. Drivers who meet the program’s criteria instantly receive the benefits.

Drivers need to collect enough points to qualify for rewards at each level. Points are earned by completing rides. The most points can be earned during peak hours when the ride demand is high.

All points reset to 0 on the 1st of each month. The level remains active from when the driver unlocks it until the end of the following month. To maintain the level, they have to collect the required points for the month.

*Nominal Power*

The continuous power rating that an electric scooter’s motor can sustain indefinitely, based on thermal and electrical design limits. It represents the stable operational output where the system avoids overheating or over-stressing components.

*Maximum Power*

The peak instantaneous power the motor can briefly deliver, typically during acceleration or climbing. It is limited by factors such as motor heat tolerance and battery discharge capabilities, and cannot be maintained for extended periods.

Copying detailed update from [~accountid:712020:f0bb5bd4-3edb-4771-912b-84750794606b]  in [#martech-announcements|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02BASTMJQ4/p1739880459114609]:



{{Bayesian simulations to validate MMM V2}}

*Problem*

* We build marketing mix models (MMM) to understand the efficiency of our marketing channels. However, we have [a tough time validating the results|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5228364125/Validating+MMM+V2].
* Last year we created a [second version of our MMM|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/4931682887/Marketing+Mix+Models+v2], we call it V2. It uses a framework not common in the industry, at least no one has published about it.
* We were very confident that it was superior to the common framework for MMMs (we call it V1), but how do we prove this?

*Solution*
We use a common tool in inference: *parameter recovery*
We test if models can accurately recover the true incremental impact of marketing channels by using simulated data that mimics real-world market dynamics.
*We define the parameters that define the media impact* and check how V1 compares to V2 in recovering them. We simulate many scenarios and let the models compete with each other

*Results*

* *V2 consistently outperforms V1 in recovering the true parameters*, especially with informed priors and lower noise levels. V1 struggles to accurately recover the channel effects, even when the noise is low.
* While V1 sometimes shows a lower MAPE for overall model fit, this does not translate to better parameter inference. *This is clear evidence that relying solely on MAPE can be misleading in our MMM models (*it may mask poor performance in uncovering true channel effects).

*Next steps*

* Simulations will continuously help us understand our models better and the assumptions needed for them to give accurate results.
* The next step is to benchmark our markets to understand in which cases MMM V2 will shine and in which cases it will have a hard time.

This was a joint effort with the amazing [@anton.bugaev|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U03EDK6MDK2]

Check out the full results: [Confluence|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/5943460505/Bayesian+simulations-+parameter+recovery]

The potential is evaluation and proposal prepped here [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q3tx-dWH7ACdB160Zzj_ov2yjptFRAqJjJOoPJSyUe8/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.qxlz8m6myi3m|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q3tx-dWH7ACdB160Zzj_ov2yjptFRAqJjJOoPJSyUe8/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.qxlz8m6myi3m|smart-link] 

*Key Proposal Insight:*

*We believe Performance Marketing*, particularly Ads, should broaden its focus beyond pure acquisition to also target the *re-activation of churned customers*. There’s a significant opportunity here—re-activation efforts (in addition to comms, discounts, and organic methods) could deliver an impact comparable to regular Ads, especially in mature markets where we no longer able to attract completely new users.

*Impact Estimations*

Rider churn is a significant challenge for Bolt, with an estimated *50 to 64 million** churned riders across all markets. That is comparable to the total number of active riders which is between *70 to 75 million**, highlighting a substantial pool of users who could be reactivated.

Based on extrapolation from the analyzed markets, the total opportunity for reactivation campaigns ranges from *0.3% (pessimistic scenario) to 10.4% (optimistic scenario)* uplift of total yearly Ride-Hailing GMV in our core markets. This translates to potential yearly GMV uplift between *€16.7M and €623.1M.*

For context: The impact of current Performance marketing, targeted at primary activations, is *±€280M* (extrapolated from measured uplift). At total budget *±€40M* with an average iROI = 7

Hi! 

Bolt does not issue invoices on behalf of restaurants, so we are unable to include a Bolt discount on the restaurant’s invoice, even if we wanted to.

Additionally, Bolt does not operate as a food reseller. This means we cannot purchase food at full price and then sell it at a discounted rate to customers.

Since Bolt does not provide any direct services to eaters, we also cannot issue a credit note to them, as there is no original invoice from us that could be credited.

Our promocodes function as a means of payment, similar to a friend giving the eater some money to help pay their bill. The restaurant still receives full payment, so the invoice correctly reflects the total order value.

If having an invoice that does not match the amount paid is a serious issue for the client, they may prefer not to use promocodes. In that case, the invoice will directly reflect their full payment. 

One alternative (which would require development) would be to provide an informal statement showing a breakdown such as:

* Order total: €10
* Amount paid by eater: €8
* Bolt subsidy: €2

However, since this would not be a legally valid invoice, it’s unclear whether this would satisfy the client. Given that, we don’t have strong grounds to justify investing in this.

** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund

[~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] Re if we would choose to launch the new fee 1 month prior to being compliant with the operating model.

# There should be assurances from all the stakeholders (such as Legal, Commerce etc) that the operating model will be brought into compliance by this internal deadline, incl if needed the project added to MVRA. 
# Re likelihood of the new platform fee triggering scrutiny, incl potentially scrutiny towards the operating model - practically I see it more as a risk assessment by Bolt local Operations together with local Legal. This is why:

* We can assess the risk based on previous experience introducing new fees to consumers. How likely is it that the new fee will increase customer incidents which may be escalated to local consumer protection authorities; how likely is it that drivers may raise issues due to them collecting and "giving away" the platform fee in case of cash rides; do we have any indication that the local consumer protection board prioritizes similar platform fees; from the customer reaction window, do we view the 1 month as a sufficiently short period in context of a new fee.
* Re FinReg licensing risk specific assessment, because we use GMV based prioritisation globally for our markets, the full financial services regulatory mapping for Ireland has not been done yet. This means that today we don't have any special knowledge of the Irish financial services regulator's supervisory priorities, or approaches to non-compliance measures. Here is our [+general risk assessment+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/3940221019/Key+Risks+Overview#What%E2%80%99s-on-stake%3F]. My guess would be that if any issues should arise due to the new fee, it would be rather the 'medium impact scenario', *provided that* we have an actual action plan in the works with reasonable deadlines to ensure op model compliance. At the moment I assume that the deadline is 1 May.

    where to_agent_type = 'ride_hailing_fleet'
    and period_start_date >= date('2016-01-01') -- when data load became consistent
    group by 1
),
last_invoice as (
select
row_number() over (partition by period_end_date, from_agent_type, from_agent_id, to_agent_type, to_agent_id order by invoice_id desc) as row_num,
*
from {{ source("dbt_billing", "etl_billing_invoicing_rides_driver_commission") }}
where created_date >= date('{{ var("data_interval_start") }}') - interval '{{ var("offset_date") }}' day - interval '365' day
    and created_date < date('{{ var("data_interval_end") }}') + interval '1' day
),
invoicing_strategy_company as (
        select distinct
        ifc.city_id,
        ifc.country_code,
        ifc.company_id,
        ifc.fee_calculator_id,
        ifc.invoicing_strategy,
        cf.min_invoice_date,
        ifc.start_date,
        date(coalesce(max(ifc.end_date) over (partition by ifc.company_id, ifc.city_id, ifc.fee_calculator_id), current_date())) as end_date,
        ifc.invoice_issuer_id,
        iii.has_single_commission_invoice_row,
        iii.rider_discount_netting
    from {{ source("dbt_billing", "etl_billing_invoicing_fee_calculator_daily") }} as ifc
    left join {{ source("invoicing", "invoicing_invoice_issuer") }} as iii on ifc.invoice_issuer_id = iii.id
    left join {{ source("admin", "admin_system_city") }} as sc on sc.id = ifc.city_id
    left join company_filter as cf on cf.company_id = ifc.company_id 
    inner join {{ ref("_rhb_country_date_switch") }} as rhb on rhb.country_code = ifc.country_code 
                                                            and ifc.date < date(from_utc_timestamp(rhb.rhb_switch_date, sc.timezone))
    where ifc.invoicing_strategy = 'company'
    and ifc.date >= cf.min_invoice_date
),
fees_company as (

        f.id,

        ic.external_id as company_id,
        ic.country as country_code,
        isc.city_id,
        f.invoice_id,
        f.currency,
        f.type as transaction_type,
        f.title as transaction_title,

* Fleet Owner and Fleet Manager is the same user type. Hi all, jumping in on this from the Privacy side.

As noted in the ticket description, we have seen a few tickets recently from riders who are asking why we need a copy of their ID in the context of the WfW category, and how we keep their data safe (see e.g. [+LSS-46368+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-46368] , [+LSS-46384+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-46384] , [+LSS-45782+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-45782], [+LSS-45782+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-45782], [+LSS-46521+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-46521]).

Regarding how to respond to the concern of *why we require a copy of the user’s ID*, we can leverage the following language (which borrows from the passenger privacy notice)

{quote}_Please note that Bolt collects certain information about you, including your profile data and identification / verification data, to enhance the safety of its passengers and drivers. It is in Bolt’s legitimate interests (and the interests of its passengers) to enhance the safety and security of the Bolt services by offering safety functionalities. Further information can be found in our privacy notice available at_ [_https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides_|https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides] _._{quote}

Regarding how to respond to the concern of *how we protect data*, we can again borrow language from the privacy notice:

{quote}_The security of your personal data is very important to us, and we have implemented appropriate technical and organisational controls to protect your personal data against unauthorised processing and against accidental loss, damage or destruction. We have implemented data encryption in transit and at rest, data privacy and security training, information security policies and controls around the confidentiality, integrity and availability of our data/systems. Any personal data collected in the course of providing Bolt services is transferred to and stored in our data centres which are located within the EEA. Only authorised employees of ​Bolt Group companies and partners ​have access to the personal data and they may access the data only for the purpose of resolving issues associated with the use of the services._{quote}

 Regarding how to respond to the concern of *whether we can store the ID*:

* I agree that we should check whether there are any such prohibitions under local Polish law. [~accountid:712020:a9ca1df5-fe05-4efc-9bb7-f89fd653ec94] I would also be grateful if you could check if there is anything under Polish law that requires us to _retain_ copies of ID used for this purpose for a certain period of time, as this would be helpful for dealing with other similar cases.
* [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] when WfW was originally assessed, were retention periods considered? I understand that we only ask for a copy of a user’s ID once for WfW (and do not trigger verification for users who have verified themselves before) - If so, is there not an argument for retaining copies of the ID for a certain period of time? Otherwise, if we no longer have the copy on record, how can we be sure that the user has properly passed verification? Surely not retaining the ID would mean we would need to re-trigger verification the next time the user wants to us WfW?
* If we are not prohibited from storing the ID, but are also not required to retain it, then IMO we should retain it unless we receive a valid deletion request from the user; in which case we can follow our usual processes and delete the ID from our systems. LMKWYT.

In this situation, an employer may terminate an employment agreement in two ways.

h3. *1. Personal Conditioned Dismissal*

An employer may terminate an employee’s contract if they fail to fulfill their work obligations due to insufficient skills, lack of knowledge, or inadequate qualifications, and if this is not due to the employee’s fault. This type of dismissal requires:

* A prior warning to the employee about unsatisfactory performance.
* An adjustment period or additional training if possible.
* Compliance with the notice period, unless otherwise specified by a collective agreement or employment contract.
* Severance pay, if the employee has been employed for at least two years.

h3. *2. Dismissal Due to Misconduct (Disciplinary Dismissal)*

If an employee fails to fulfill their work obligations due to negligence, irresponsible work, or refusal to perform tasks, the employer may dismiss them for misconduct. In this case:

* The employee must first receive a written warning with an opportunity to correct their behavior (unless the violation is severe).
* If the employee does not improve, the employer may proceed with dismissal.
* Immediate dismissal (without notice) can be given if the misconduct is exceptionally severe.

The law does not specify an exact number of days but states that the employee must be given a reasonable period to correct their behavior. In practice, this period usually lasts:

* 8 to 15 days for minor violations of work obligations.
* 30 days or more for complex work tasks requiring more time for improvement.

If the employee fails to improve within the given period, the employer may proceed with regular dismissal.

If the violation of work obligations is particularly severe (e.g., theft, violence, abuse of position), the employer may issue an immediate dismissal without prior warning and without a notice period.



Please note that in both cases the employee can challenge the dismissal in court within 15 days of receiving the dismissal notice.

If the court finds the dismissal unlawful, it may order:

* Reinstatement of the employee.
* Compensation for lost wages and damages.

Therefore, to prevent any potential claims, we always recommend signing a settlement with the employee, granting them the same rights they would have received in the case of dismissal. #* R2M's fee is 1% of the total funding requested.
#* Invoice issued within 30 days of submission, payable within 30 days.
#* Late payment incurs a 1% monthly penalty.
# *Confidentiality*
#* Both parties must protect confidential information for three years after the agreement ends.
#* Certain exceptions apply (e.g., publicly available or independently developed information).
# *Warranties & Limitations of Liability*
#* No guarantee of success for the proposal.
#* R2M’s liability is limited to revising/replacing work or refunding fees paid, with no liability for indirect damages.
# *Termination*
#* The agreement remains in effect until the proposal is submitted.
#* Either party may terminate immediately if the other party materially breaches the contract and fails to remedy it within 30 business days.



*Points for Attention:*

*No Guarantee of Funding Success*
The agreement clearly specifies that R2M does not guarantee funding success.

*Limited Liability of R2M*
The liability cap, which limits R2M’s responsibility to the refund of fees paid, may leave Bolt without full compensation if the work is deemed inadequate. However, this limitation appears reasonable under the circumstances.

*Late Payment Penalty*
A 1% monthly late payment fee will apply if Bolt does not make payment on time. 

*→ Recommendation:* I would suggest pushing back on this penalty.

*Confidentiality Considerations*
Bolt must ensure all sensitive data is properly marked as "confidential" to ensure protection under the agreement. Failure to do so may result in potential confidentiality breaches.

*Termination Clause Considerations*
The clause limits Bolt’s ability to terminate the agreement unless there is a material breach that remains unresolved for 30 business days. This could reduce flexibility if circumstances change and Bolt no longer wishes to proceed with the contract.

*→ Recommendation:* including a _termination for convenience_ clause. This would allow Bolt to terminate the agreement without cause, providing greater flexibility should the circumstances change during the contract term.

Hi [~accountid:712020:80adc2a7-05ca-4e9d-b299-6ace53125c4f] , thank you for flagging this initiative to me. 

* You can share *anonymous* rider feedback with drivers that affects their services.
* You may also share the so-called reclassification-risky comments, as they still impact the rating. If the driver is unaware of them, they might lack sufficient information to improve. The key point here is how we communicate this - by sharing the feedback, Bolt is not imposing requirements on drivers (they can, in practice, disregard it), but rather ensuring greater transparency by providing information that could benefit the driver. This, in turn, leads to happier clients, increased platform usage, more rides for drivers, a higher earning (due to the high prices in HVC) and a higher chance of receiving tips.
However, as correctly stated in the Excel file, reclassification-risky comments alone cannot be the sole reason *for suspending* a driver. {color:#403294}_But we are only discussing removal from a category, client feedback that does not meet the requirements of certain categories could be used as a basis for removal, even if it includes reclassification-risky comments. Still, to mitigate any risks, it would be better to combine both reclassification-risky and non-reclassification-risky comments to justify removal from HVC._{color}

* Some legal considerations:
** We *cannot* block a driver *solely* for a low rating. Suspension is only justified if *the low rating is accompanied by a complaint* (e.g., a comment from the client).  I would apply the same logic for removal from HVC. 
** Additionally:
*** *P2B Regulation* requires platform operators to maintain a fair, transparent, and accountable relationship with business users (couriers) and consumers.
*** *EE Consumer Protection Act, Art. 9 (1)* entitles consumers to receive services of certain quality: _“Goods and_ *_services shall_* _meet the established requirements, be harmless to the life, health and property of the consumer if used for their intended purpose and_ *_have the characteristics which can normally be expected of them by consumers_*_”._ As a platform, we must ensure that services provided through Bolt meet reasonable consumer expectations. 

Thus, removal from HVC could be justified based on consumer rights and their expectations of a certain service level in HVC.
